facts.statement: The genus Yungavolucris was described by Chiappe in 1993.
Yungavolucris brevipedalis lived during the Late Cretaceous (Maastrichtian), approximately 70.6 to 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Yungavolucris is a genus of enantiornitheans. It contains the single species Yungavolucris brevipedalis, which lived in the Late Cretaceous (Maastrichtian, c.70.6 – 66 mya).

facts.statement: Fossil bones of Yungavolucris were discovered in the Lecho Formation at estancia El Brete, Argentina.
facts.quote: The fossil bones were found in the Lecho Formation at estancia El Brete, Argentina.

facts.statement: The name Yungavolucris brevipedalis translates to "Short-footed Yungas bird".
The tarsometatarsals of Yungavolucris are unusually stout, flat, and very wide at the lower end.
facts.quote: These tarsometatarsals are unusually very stout and flat, and also very wide at the lower end.

facts.statement: The known fossil specimens of Yungavolucris are small, measuring just over 4 cm (1.5 inches) in length.
facts.quote: These specimens are small, just over 4 cm (1.5 inches) long

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that if the legs were only shortened but not widened, Yungavolucris might have been a large chicken-sized bird (50 cm long, 25 cm high, 1.75 kg) that was heavily built, sluggish, and possibly flightless.
facts.quote: Thus, if the leg and foot only shortened and did not also become wider, it might be expected to have been a heavily built, sluggish and maybe even flightless bird the size of a large chicken: a length of 50 cm (20 in), hip height of 25 cm (10 in), and weight of 1.75 kg (4 lb).

facts.statement: Metatarsal IV is very thin and diminished but is about the same length as metatarsal III.
facts.quote: Metatarsal IV (the outermost bone of the tarsometatarsus) is very thin and diminished, but nevertheless about the same length as metatarsal III (the middle bone of the tarsometatarsus).

facts.statement: Metatarsal II possesses a very broad and pulley-shaped trochlea, which is the toe joint.
facts.quote: Metatarsal II (the innermost preserved bone of the tarsometatarsus) has a very broad and pulley-shaped trochlea (toe joint).

facts.statement: A small bony bump, known as a dorsomedial projection, is located just above the inside edge of the trochlea on metatarsal II.
facts.quote: A small bony bump (a dorsomedial projection) is present just above the inside edge of this trochlea.

facts.statement: No metatarsal I or hallux has been preserved in any Yungavolucris specimens.
facts.quote: No metatarsal I or hallux is preserved in any of the specimens.

facts.statement: Some studies have recovered Yungavolucris as a close relative of Grabauornis.
facts.quote: A few studies have recovered it as a close relative of Grabauornis.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Yungavolucris is the same species as other El Brete enantiornitheans known only from forelimb bones, since only the tarsometatarsus is known for Yungavolucris.
facts.quote: As only the tarsometatarsus is known from Yungavolucris, it might be the same species as one of the other El Brete enantiornitheans described based on forelimb bones.

facts.statement: Yungavolucris belongs to the subclass Enantiornithes.
Yungavolucris is an extinct genus of avialans belonging to the clade Enantiornithes that inhabited Argentina during the Upper Cretaceous.
facts.quote: Yungavolucris es un género extinto de avialano perteneciente al clado Enantiornithes que habitó Argentina durante el Cretácico Superior.

facts.statement: The time range for Yungavolucris is the Maastrichtian, from 72.2 to 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Maastrichtian to Maastrichtian (72.2 to 66 million years ago)

rejected.statement: The end of metatarsal III is bent outwards to a position that would normally fall between toes 3 and 4 in other birds.
rejected.quote: In addition, the end of metatarsal III is bent outwards, to a position that would in other birds fall between toes 3 and 4.
